items.title: Toward an AI- and learning-analytics-enabled inclusive support framework for students with learning difficulties in Kuwait's higher education institutions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are transforming higher education by enabling personalised learning, adaptive support, and data-informed decision-making. These developments present significant opportunities for improving educational inclusion for students with learning difficulties, yet they also introduce challenges relating to privacy, algorithmic bias, explainability, accessibility, and governance. Although Kuwait has strengthened disability legislation while simultaneously investing in AI-enabled education under Kuwait Vision 2035, these policy agendas have largely evolved independently. Similar governance gaps are evident across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), where disability inclusion, AI adoption, and higher education reform remain weakly integrated. This conceptual paper develops the AI- and Learning-Analytics-Enabled Inclusive Support Framework for Learning Difficulties (ISF-LD) to guide the responsible implementation of AI within inclusive higher education. Using a conceptual framework development methodology, the study synthesises evidence from four complementary domains: research on learning difficulties and disability inclusion; scholarship on AI, learning analytics, and responsible AI; national and international policy documents; and established educational and disability theories. The framework is informed by six theoretical perspectives: the Social Model of Disability, Universal Design for Learning, Sociocultural Theory, Self-Determination Theory, learning analytics ethics, and responsible AI principles. The proposed framework comprises five interconnected implementation layers: national policy and governance, institutional leadership and disability services, faculty capability, AI-enabled inclusive pedagogy and assessment, and student self-determination. These layers operate through an iterative, non-linear governance model in which each layer informs and is informed by the others, supported by four cross-cutting principles: rights-based governance, stigma-aware disclosure, universal accessibility, and responsible AI. Together, they position AI as a governed educational capability that supports inclusion while safeguarding learner autonomy, transparency, and institutional accountability. The paper contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it integrates disability studies, AI governance, learning analytics, and inclusive higher education within a single conceptual model. Second, it addresses an important policy gap by linking disability inclusion with AI governance in the context of Kuwait and the GCC. Third, it proposes a theoretically grounded and empirically testable framework that can inform institutional strategy, educational policy, and future research on responsible AI in higher education. Although developed within Kuwait, the ISF-LD offers a transferable governance model for universities seeking to implement AI ethically while advancing equitable and inclusive learning.

items.title: Towards the learning estate: from digital–physical to experience orchestration
items.abstract: Universities increasingly orchestrate teaching and learning through compound configurations that span spaces, devices, timetables and roles. As digital content and workflows increasingly shape physical estates, and vice versa, alignment frames overlook the compound, cross-host configurations already in motion. In this article we ask whether estate-level orchestration, rather than digital–physical alignment alone, should be the operative unit of design for planning and delivering student experiences across and beyond campus. We draw on three exemplars at a research-intensive university: (1) a theatre-scale interactive three-dimensional system, which streams or web-delivers interactive three-dimension into traditional lecture theatres and learners’ devices; (2) a high-fidelity virtual reality digital twin of a chemistry lab for pre-lab rehearsal; and (3) space-planning web apps for co-design and decision support. From these, we sketch a purpose-orientated, configuration-first stance and situate it within work on cyber-/smart-campus estates, learning ecologies, TPACK and postdigital perspectives. Beyond education, digital-first space planning is already operational at scale, including in automotive manufacturing (BMW Group), cultural architecture (Dubai Museum of the Future) and national infrastructure (National Grid’s Triton platform). Higher education has both the conceptual case and, in several respects, the enabling conditions to follow. Hence, we argue that the convergence of immersive, computational and spatial technologies is expanding what institutions can compose and deliver, making device-label categories less useful for both learning and space design. This configuration-first stance is also directly applicable to the governance of artificial intelligence in higher education: as with earlier technology labels, institutions risk misallocating attention and resource if ‘artificial intelligence’ is treated as a discrete category rather than as a family of capabilities, from generative code or audiovisual models to computer vision and wearable ‘artificial intelligence’, some of which already permeate the configurations described here. We conclude with operational implications and a call for institutions to transcend their siloed functions and budgets, by elevating orchestration (not devices, spaces or platforms) as the primary unit of design.

items.title: Trust and Adoption Intention Toward AI-Enabled IBM Cloud Services Among IT Professionals in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial-intelligence-enabled cloud services are becoming increasingly important for digital transformation, but users may not adopt these services simply because they believe the technology is useful. This study examines the factors associated with adoption intention toward AI-enabled IBM Cloud services in Bangladesh, with particular attention to performance expectations, trust, technology readiness and digital skills readiness. The analysis uses the Group 5 survey database, which contains 400 records. After applying the prespecified attention-check criterion, 385 cases were retained for the main analysis. The database contains 30 five-point Likert-scale items representing 10 constructs: perceived usefulness, relative advantage, compatibility, innovation adoption readiness, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, trust, technology readiness, digital skills readiness and adoption intention. Descriptive statistics, reliability and measurement diagnostics, hierarchical regression, bootstrap analysis and importance-performance analysis were used to examine the data. Overall adoption intention was positive (M=3.79, SD=0.48). The full regression model explained 30.5% of the variance in adoption intention. Technology readiness was the strongest unique predictor (β=.224, p<.001), followed by performance expectancy (β=.157, p=.001), digital skills readiness (β=.147, p=.002) and trust (β=.140, p=.003). Adding the trust and readiness variables increased the explained variance by 11.6 percentage points (ΔR²=.116), showing that these factors provide important information beyond innovation attributes and UTAUT-oriented expectations. An exploratory indirect pathway was also observed: technology readiness was positively related to digital skills readiness, which was in turn related to adoption intention. The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (ab=.067, 95% CI [.031, .108]). These findings suggest that AI-enabled cloud adoption is not only a question of perceived technological value; it also depends on whether users feel prepared, digitally capable and sufficiently confident in the cloud provider. However, all ten three-item scales showed Cronbach's alpha values below .70, and several discriminant-validity indicators were elevated. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as data-grounded associations rather than as definitive confirmation of a latent-variable model. items.title: Trust of Pre-Service Teachers in Government Response to Gen AI Generated Deepfakes
items.abstract: This study examined the perceptions of pre-service teachers regarding the Spanish government’s response to the misuse of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) for creating disinformation, as well as the mitigation of risks associated with deepfakes produced using these digital tools. A quantitative methodology was employed, involving 133 pre-service teachers pursuing a Primary Education degree in the Region of Murcia (Spain) who participated voluntarily. The results revealed low levels of confidence in the government’s response to these online threats. However, a minority of participants expressed greater confidence in the government and focused more on the risk of generative AI being misused to amplify manipulative disinformation campaigns. Raising awareness about the link between pre-service teachers’ knowledge of this issue and the government’s response could prompt educational authorities to take action and establish boundaries regarding the weaponisation potential of deepfakes. Specifically, further research within higher education programs is needed to help students master digital citizenship competencies that enable them to identify tactics of digital political manipulation, evaluate the motivations underlying the sources, and adopt preventive tracking mechanisms to rebuild the trust in authentic political information digitally accessible.

items.title: Usability Challenges across AI-Assisted Infrastructure, Security, and Scientific Workflows
items.abstract: AI-assisted tooling is increasingly being integrated into infrastructure management, security operations, software engineering, and scientific computing environments. While discussion around AI adoption often emphasizes automation and productivity, expert users still need to understand what these systems are doing, decide when to trust their recommendations, and know what to do when the system is wrong or uncertain. This talk synthesizes findings and observations from UX research across enterprise data classification, identity and access management (IAM), backup and recovery, ransomware resilience, and AI-assisted infrastructure workflows. The evidence includes studies with cloud developers, security and compliance practitioners, and IT and site reliability professionals, alongside ongoing design and research work examining how expert users interact with AI-supported technical systems. Across these domains, three recurring usability challenges emerge: unclear system state, difficulty evaluating AI-generated recommendations, and limited support for correcting or recovering from AI-supported actions when something goes wrong. Although the technical environments differ, users repeatedly need to understand what the system observed or changed, evaluate whether a recommendation is appropriate for their specific context, and determine what to verify, reverse, or escalate before taking consequential action. These challenges have direct implications for research software engineering. AI-assisted code generation, workflow scripting, cloud and HPC configuration, notebook assistants, debugging, testing, and scientific automation introduce similar questions about visibility, trust, accountability, and recoverability. Lessons from enterprise infrastructure and security therefore provide useful design considerations for RSEs evaluating or building AI-assisted research software. The session offers a cross-domain synthesis of these recurring human-AI interaction challenges and practical questions for evaluating AI-assisted systems. Attendees will leave with a set of questions they can use to evaluate AI-assisted systems: whether users can understand system state, decide when to rely on a recommendation and when to question it, intervene when necessary, and verify or recover from the resulting actions. Connection to Mission, Goals, & Interests of US-RSE Community This talk aligns closely with the USRSE’26 theme, “Advancing Science in the Age of AI,” by focusing on the human and operational challenges that emerge as AI-assisted tooling is integrated into technical and scientific workflows. My background is in UX research and human factors across enterprise infrastructure, cloud systems, security tooling, and scientific software environments. Across these domains, I have observed the same challenges emerge when expert users interact with AI systems, including issues with transparency, trust calibration, oversight, error recovery, and workflow integration. While conversations around AI often emphasize capability and productivity, this session examines how usability and human-centered design influence the successful adoption of AI within complex environments. These topics are directly relevant to research software engineers who develop, evaluate, maintain, or adopt AI-assisted tools as part of scientific workflows. The goal of this session is to encourage discussion around designing AI systems that better support expert users while maintaining reliability, transparency, and human understanding. These topics connect strongly with the US-RSE community’s broader interests in sustainable, usable, and effective research software.

items.title: Use of a GenAI-patient for medical communication training for undergraduate medical students—a quasi-experimental study
items.abstract: Background Effective communication is fundamental to high-quality healthcare. Communication skills training is a core component of medical curricula, yet opportunities to practice with standardized patients (SPs) are limited, costly, and can elicit anxiety in novice learners. Generative AI (GenAI) virtual patients may offer a scalable and accessible supplement. This quasi-experimental study examined the effect of practicing with a GenAI-patient on medical students’ self-reported nervousness, preparedness, self-efficacy, and self-perceived competence during their first SP encounter. Materials and methods First-year medical students ( n = 383) at the University of Amsterdam were allocated on the basis of the class schedule to a control group receiving standard e-learning preparation ( n = 182) or an intervention group offered voluntary additional access to a GenAI-patient built on a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework using GPT-4o ( n = 201). Students completed a 31-item questionnaire after their first SP class. Primary outcomes were nervousness, preparedness, self-efficacy, and self-perceived competence. Group differences were assessed using Mann–Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The primary analysis was by intention-to-treat, comparing all students allocated to the intervention with all control students; the comparison restricted to actual users of the tool was secondary. Results Of 180 students that completed the questionnaire, 84 were controls and 96 students were allocated to the intervention, of whom 49 had used the GenAI-patient. No statistically significant differences were found between groups on the outcomes after FDR correction. In the intention-to-treat analysis; all composite effect sizes were near zero (Cliff's delta −0.05 to 0.04, all 95% confidence intervals including zero), as were those in the per-protocol comparison (−0.12 to 0.07). Among tool users, experience was generally positive: 63%–71% gave positive ratings. The majority considered the GenAI-patient a valuable contribution to the standard class preparation (71%). Conclusions Voluntary, single-session text-based practice with a GenAI-patient did not significantly reduce nervousness or improve self-assessed communication competence before a first SP encounter. Positive user experience suggests potential for the format, provided future iterations incorporate mandatory minimum engagement, multiple patient cases, automated feedback, and higher-fidelity multimodal interaction.

items.title: Use of AI in research
items.abstract: This lecture for MSc students in aerospace engineering presents a workflow for research with AI agents, from the author's evaluation of large language models between ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, and Claude Opus 5.5. A use case shows an agent building a verified and validated Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam benchmarks of Krueger (2008) in one morning, with the researcher answering the decisive questions at checkpoints. The lecture discusses the responsible use of AI, how AI changes highly technical work, the growing role of experiments, and what this means for junior engineers. Lecture Given on 19 October 2026 as part of the Aerospace Structures and Materials core, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands. Contents Motivation for this lecture: why, after evaluating the new large language models every summer, Claude Opus 5 (August 2026) changed the author's way of working, and why the lecture was given now. Learning objectives: understand, evaluate and apply the author's way of working with novel AI models; create your own way of working with them; re-evaluate the role of a junior engineer in a world with AI. A brief history of large language models: from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-4 (2023). How AI entered my research/education workflows: ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5, and an analogy of three kinds of helpers. What fits inside current LLMs: tokens, context windows measured in papers, parameters against context, and the context of one agent session. Responsible use of AI: three rules, with a discussion: "Everything that can be automated should be automated"; "Focus on the crucial things, avoid the trivial things"; "Never delegate the decisions that make your work yours". My workflow with AI: a working folder in an integrated development environment, Claude as the agent, an HPC cluster as the simulation environment, and the state of the work kept in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat. Consequences of a workflow with AI: how research moves forward through verification, validation and new hypotheses; where AI can take over parts of this process; what changed in the author's work. Use case: a verified DCB model: the prompt (goal, ten ground rules, phases with checkpoints), one morning by the clock, and where the model stood at the end of it. Figures as code: TikZ: vector figures written by the agent from the models' own data. How has AI changed highly technical jobs: numerical work and theoretical research; the shift from executing calculations to synthesis and verification; why experiments matter more, including AI combined with mechanical testing. The AI workflow of a junior engineer: how engineers grew until about 2024, judging what the AI produces, and two discussions. Take-home messages. The use case The agent built an Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam (DCB) benchmarks of the NASA report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, following a prompt written as a contract: every value with its source, every analysis through scripts, failed runs kept, and stops at two checkpoints where the researcher decides. In one morning, the agent completed the environment check and the reference card (09:46 to 10:07), wrote the plan after the researcher's decisions at the first checkpoint (11:23 to 11:29), and built and verified the model after the second checkpoint: the first models ran at 12:07, and the model worked at 13:23. At that point, the unidirectional model agreed with the published Marc 3D results of Orifici and Krueger (2010) within 0.1 to 0.6 %, and with the 2008 report within 0.1 to 0.8 % once its crack fronts were taken 0.5 mm beyond the labelled lengths; the acceptance criterion of the approved plan was 2 %. Running the use case The file use-case.zip contains the prompt of the use case, PROMPT_use_case.md. The report it works from is not included; to run the use case: Download the report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, from the NASA Technical Reports Server, where it is available free of charge: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20080015439. In your project folder, create a subfolder named references and save the report there as references/krueger2008NASA.pdf. The file name is the key of the case: if the agent does not find this file, it stops and asks. Place the prompt in the project folder, and check that its cluster settings suit your environment: ground rule 4 submits every analysis with qsub, and Phase 0 loads Abaqus in the cluster. Open the project folder with an AI coding agent (in the lecture: Claude, in an integrated development environment), and ask it to read the prompt and start with Phase 0. The agent creates the case folder krueger2008NASA_dcb next to references, and stops at two checkpoints for your decisions. Requirements: Abaqus with a valid licence, including its Python for scripting and post-processing; a computer or cluster to run the analyses; and Python for the work outside Abaqus, such as digitising figures. Take-home messages Write the prompt as a contract: definitions, ground rules, phases, and checkpoints where the agent stops and asks. Keep the state in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat: someone else can reproduce every number. Automate everything that can be automated, and keep the focus on the crucial things. Let the agent verify and look for evidence; you judge the evidence. Delegate the implementation and the evidence for verification; keep the validation, the new hypotheses and the decisions at the checkpoints. Numerical work is increasingly automated, and theory is reaching automated scale: the work shifts to synthesis and problem definition, and to verification and auditing, and experiments matter more. For junior engineers: invest in the fundamentals; make a real effort to check what the AI produces against independent references; if you are not sure about a decision, study and talk to more experienced peers. Questions for discussion What do you consider a responsible use of AI? Which tasks of your work are trivial, and which are crucial? Which decisions make your work yours? In the process of doing research, where do you think we can delegate to AI? How can a recently graduated student judge what the AI produces and answer the decisive questions? How can a junior engineer work in synthesis and problem definition, and in verification and auditing of what an AI model does and produces, without the experience of a senior engineer, and without the chance to gain it the conventional way? items.title: Using AI to Build Student Feedback Literacy and Leverage Assessment as a Learning Tool
items.abstract: This conceptual article explores practical ways in which college and university instructors can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment as learning and develop students’ feedback literacy. Traditional assessment practices often focus on assessment for learning (informing instruction) or of learning (measuring outcomes), while assessment as learning—when students actively monitor and reflect on their own learning—receives less attention. AI can help instructors leverage assessment as a learning tool by generating work samples for student analysis and providing timely, actionable feedback that students can use to revise their work. When combined with instructor modeling, peer dialogue, and scaffolds such as guiding questions or graphic organizers, AI-supported feedback promotes metacognition, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation skills. The article provides practical guidance, including prompts and strategies for using AI to enhance student engagement with feedback, helping instructors create more efficient, effective, and student-centered practices that utilize assessments as learning tools.

items.title: What Happens When Generative AI Enters College Data Analysis Education? Evaluating Changes in Students' Academic Self-Efficacy, Self-Regulated Learning, and Engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support learning in higher education, but evidence regarding changes in students' academic self-efficacy, self-regulated learning, and academic engagement remains limited. This study examined changes associated with a six-week generative AI-based data analysis education program among students at a three-year college in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China. A one-group pretest-posttest design was employed. Of 210 questionnaires distributed, 202 valid paired responses were analyzed. Academic self-efficacy, self-regulated learning, and academic engagement were measured using five-point Likert scales, with adapted items informed by established instruments. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlations, and paired-samples t tests were conducted. All three outcomes increased significantly: academic self-efficacy from 3.21 to 3.48 (dz = 0.38), self-regulated learning from 3.18 to 3.52 (dz = 0.51), and academic engagement from 3.35 to 3.66 (dz = 0.44). Posttest correlations among the outcomes were positive (r = 0.56-0.65, all p < .001). These findings suggest that structured AI-supported data analysis instruction may accompany improvements in students' confidence, learning regulation, and engagement. However, the one-group design cannot isolate the causal contribution of generative AI from other elements of the instructional program. items.title: What makes human service distinctly human in the AI era? Conceptualizing and measuring authentic relational service competency
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) service agents increasingly simulate human interaction, the basis for distinguishing human service has become theoretically ambiguous. While prior research consistently identifies authenticity as a key limitation of AI-enabled service, authenticity remains underdeveloped as a uniquely human service capability. Addressing this gap, we introduce Authentic Relational Service (ARS) as a distinct form of service through which frontline employees create genuine, contextually responsive, and relationship-centered customer interactions. We further conceptualize authenticity as a competency-based capability and develop a measure of Authentic Relational Service Competency (ARSC), which enables frontline employees to enact ARS. Using established scale-development procedures, this study identifies and validates four dimensions of ARSC: perspective-taking, patience, creativity, and agility. By conceptualizing and operationalizing Authentic Relational Service as a distinct human service capability, this research advances theory on human-AI service differentiation and provides a foundation for understanding uniquely human value creation in service contexts.

items.title: When creativity meets artificial intelligence: a sequential path to smart learning and academic performance
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and students' creative thinking (CT) contribute to smart learning (SL) and academic performance (AP) in higher education. It further examines whether AI use and SL mediate the relationship between CT and AP in a sequential manner. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was adopted, and data were collected from 227 university students in Bangladesh. Structural equation modelling with SmartPLS was used to evaluate the proposed relationships. Findings The results show that both AI usage and CT are positively and significantly related to SL and AP. Beyond these direct associations, the data also point to a meaningful serial mediation pathway: students with stronger CT tend to report greater AI usage, which is in turn associated with higher SL engagement, and this heightened engagement is associated with better AP. Originality/value This study uniquely links CT, AI use, SL and AP in Bangladeshi higher education. It shows how CT affects academic achievement through sequential paths of AI usage and SL, clarifying how student talents convert into outcomes in digital learning environments. The findings suggest that institutions should promote CT and use AI-based learning tools to improve student performance.

items.title: When Should AI Chime In? Benchmarking Timely Contribution of Proactive Agents in Multi-Party Chat
items.abstract: Proactive agents can support group collaboration by surfacing useful information without waiting to be asked, but even relevant contributions can be disruptive if poorly timed. In this work, we isolate the timing question: given a fixed candidate contribution such as a clarification or relevant fact, when should an AI agent chime in? We introduce PITCH (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat), to our knowledge the first benchmark with large-scale human judgments of proactive agent timing collected from participants in the same unscripted multi-party conversations they took part in. To collect high-quality judgments, we design a novel interface in which 2-4 people chat synchronously, author candidate AI contribution messages, place their own and others' contributions into the chat history, and then deliberate as a group about the best placement for each message. PITCH contains 384 candidate contributions and 1,091 judgments, each marking an ideal turn, an acceptable window, or that a contribution should not appear, from 89 participants engaged in 35 conversations. Evaluating 15 models across 28 configurations, we find that while models can place contributions well when given the entire conversation history, they systematically chime in too early when asked to decide live as the conversation unfolds: best-turn accuracy falls from 57.8% to 19.0%, with nearly half of placements occurring before every participant's acceptable window. In comparison, lay humans deciding live are more accurate (23.7% vs 19.0%), and fewer of their placements are premature (39.7% vs 46.4%). Model reasoning traces show that 93% of intervention justifications cite relevance, while almost none consider waiting. By providing a human-grounded benchmark, our work reveals gaps in agents' ability to integrate into group settings and points towards proactive agents that can reason explicitly about appropriate timing.

items.title: Who Uses Conversational AI and Why? Distinct User Profiles and Their Links to Personality, Attachment, and Well-Being
items.abstract: With the increasing use of conversational AI (CAI) agents, such as ChatGPT, public concern about their social implications has grown. Understanding these implications requires new knowledge about the increasingly diverse motives underlying CAI use, ranging from instrumental purposes, such as work, to personal purposes, including social support and entertainment. However, little is known about the motivational profiles underlying CAI use, how these profiles relate to personality traits and attachment dimensions, or whether they differ in well-being. To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 783 CAI users (Mage = 43.46, SD = 13.58). Drawing on Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory, we measured key motivations underlying CAI use, including information seeking, task efficiency, personalization, social interaction, and playfulness, and subjected them to latent profile analysis to uncover distinct motivational profiles. Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness) and attachment styles (Anxious and Avoidant) were examined as predictors of the user profiles. We measured emotional, social, and psychological well-being to understand if these aspects differed across the various user profiles. We identified four distinct profiles of CAI users: Occasional Information Seekers, Utilitarians, Social Engagers, and All-Round Engagers. Neuroticism, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Attachment anxiety were significant predictors of profile membership. Finally, profile membership was associated with all well-being indicators, with All-Round Engagers reporting the highest well-being across all three dimensions and Social Engagers reporting the lowest emotional and psychological well-being. These findings advance our understanding of who engages with CAI and how, with potential implications for well-being.

items.title: Why the World Needs Formed Leaders Now More Than Ever: Leadership Formation in an Age of Artificial Intelligence, Accelerating Change, and Human Uncertainty
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the conditions under which leaders decide, delegate and exercise authority. Field and experimental evidence shows that generative AI can raise productivity on many knowledge tasks, but it can also lower the quality of decisions when people accept its outputs uncritically. Large practitioner surveys suggest that organizational readiness, including leadership alignment, is lagging behind individual adoption. Organizations have responded mainly by investing in skills: AI literacy, digital capability and updated competency models. This conceptual position paper argues that such investment is necessary but not sufficient. As technology widens what leaders can do, the quality of leadership depends more heavily on the leader's formation: the process through which purpose and identity are clarified and integrated, expressed as a recognizable leadership signature, and refined through ownership of the impact that leadership produces. Drawing on research into leader identity, developmental readiness, leader character, paradox, identity threat and automation bias, the paper defines leadership formation and the formed leader through the four dimensions of the Four Prints Method, a practice-derived framework: purpose, identity, signature and impact. Purpose and identity are treated as the measurable root of formation, signature as its expression and impact as its evidence. It then proposes a construct, grounded adaptability: the capacity to keep purpose, identity and ethical commitments coherent while revising strategies, methods and beliefs about means in response to new evidence. The construct is distinguished from paradox mindset, paradoxical leader behavior, organizational ambidexterity, adaptive leadership, learning agility and authentic leadership. Its proposed mechanism is the source of a leader's grounding. Grounding that rests on role-contingent attributes, such as expertise or position, is expected to make AI-driven disruption feel like a threat to identity, and so to provoke rigid or reactive responses. Grounding that rests on purpose and values is expected to support discriminating adaptation instead. The paper advances five testable propositions, specifies rival explanations and outlines research designs. Its implications for executive development, succession, AI governance and leadership education are each labelled by the strength of evidence behind them. The paper concludes that leader formation should be treated as a necessary, though not sufficient, part of preparing leaders to govern powerful technologies responsibly.

items.title: A Practitioner's Perspective on LLM-Assisted Writing: Insights on Workflow Process and Cognitive Engagement
items.abstract: The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) is groundbreaking, given their ability to produce the next most probable words near perfection according to user prompts via chatbots. This represents a capacity for cognitive reasoning in learning by selecting words strategically based on an understanding of context and intent. When an AI model reaches the point where it can organize thoughts and generate structured writing, how deliberate does the ordinary human remain in cognitive engagement and freedom of choice? This paper explicitly examines LLM-assisted writing from a practical co-partner perspective, analyzing its impact on knowledge work, the functioning of overall AI workflows, and its influence on human cognition. Recent studies on human–LLM collaboration, alongside the author's nearly half a decade of practical experience, are presented to substantiate this perspective. items.title: A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and Compliance Implications
items.abstract: Large language models now write a material and growing share of production software, including software that executes regulated financial functions.The empirical literature on their reliability has grown rapidly and is, on its own terms, sophisticated.The governance frameworks that regulated institutions must satisfy were, without exception, written for a different kind of artefact, and in the most consequential recent case, were revised in full knowledge of generative AI and deliberately declined to cover it.Objective.This review synthesises the evidence on the reliability of AI-assisted code generation, on the human factors governing its use, and on the intellectual-property and supply-chain exposures it creates; and determines how that evidence maps onto the model-risk, AI-specific and operational-resilience regimes applicable to regulated software environments.Method.We conducted a systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. and reported against PRISMA 2020, with a restricted multivocal stratum after Garousi et al. admitting regulatory instruments and supervisory guidance.Studies were appraised on an adapted Dybå-Dingsøyr instrument extended with an item recording whether deployment context or regulatory constraint is characterised.Results.Five findings.First, benchmark performance and field reliability have decoupled: correctness benchmarks are saturated and contamination-prone while defect rates measured in real repositories remain substantial, so the headline capability numbers do not license deployment inferences.Second, security evidence is mixed, controlled model evaluations report high vulnerability rates while several developer studies find little or no security penalty, and the disagreement is explained by unit of analysis rather than by any study being wrong.Third, the most robust human-factors finding is not that assisted code is worse but that developers believe it is better than it is, which relocates the risk from the artefact to the review process.Fourth, package hallucination converts a model reliability property into an attacker-controllable supply-chain channel, and is the one exposure with no human-review mitigation.Fifth, and most consequentially, the April 2026 revision of US interagency model-risk guidance explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from scope, leaving the primary supervisory framework silent on precisely this class of system. A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and ComplianceImplications; David Excel Ozowara Conclusion.We argue that AI-assisted code generation is misclassified when treated as a model-risk problem, because the model produces no decision and enters no inventory; it is better understood as a change to the software development lifecycle's assurance basis.We present the Generated Code Assurance Frame, a five-layer mapping from generation practice to the assurance claim it disturbs, and a research agenda centred on measuring review efficacy rather than generation quality.Citation

items.title: AI Driven Personalized Learning and Learning Analytics in Higher Education: Effects on Student Engagement, Achievement and Research Integrity
items.abstract: The study aimed to examine the effect of personalized learning through artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics on student engagement and learning outcomes of higher education institutes in Pakistan with implications for Research Integrity at these institutes. Adopting a mixed methods approach, quantitative data gathered from 500 students from an undergraduate science program, with semi structured interviews with 30 students for the qualitative data. The descriptive statistics indicated that the mean engagement scores for those students who have access to AI based personalized learnings were significantly higher than the mean scores of students in traditional learning setting; it is from these that an increase in engagement by the students were observed. There was an improvement in Academic achievement as well, as indicated by higher grade point averages, and improved scores of the formative assessments. The regression analysis results showed that AI (personalized learning) and learning analytics (β = .41; p < .001) were among its most important models that were significant in predicting the variable of academic achievement; the analysis of correlation results showed that there was a good positive correlation between the variables of engagement and academic achievement (r = .63, p < .01). The qualitative results corroborated this as students felt there was a significant increase in motivation, personalized feedback, and adaptive learning pathways as being the most beneficial aspects of the AI integration. Issues were identified that could interfere in successful implementation: Data privacy concerns, uneven access to technology and insufficient faculty preparation. According to this study, personalized learning & learning analytics with AI have proved to be significant drivers of student engagement & academic performance, provided that the ethical issues and infrastructure are sorted out and this may influence the way research integrity and rigor will be upheld within Higher Education Institutions. The findings herein expand the conversation taking place around the role of AI in education and highlight the need to embed learning analytics in a learning design practice, to create inclusive and effective learning spaces.

items.title: AI Pedagogy in Higher Education: A Scoping Review of Competencies, Enactments, and Ethical Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet the pedagogical field intended to organise its use remains conceptually underdeveloped. This scoping review mapped and synthesised peer-reviewed literature on AI pedagogy in higher education, using teacher education as the primary analytic lens. Following Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting principles, searches were conducted across ten databases and publisher platforms for literature published between 2022 and March 2026. Of 956 records screened, 191 studies were included. Data charting and synthesis combined deductive coding, an a priori codebook, AI-assisted coding in Atlas. ti, and human inductive open coding. Six interrelated themes emerged: AI pedagogy is contextually produced rather than universally defined; conceptualised through pedagogical integration, competence, and borrowed theories rather than a settled standalone theory; enacted mainly through augmentation-oriented practices and generative AI tools; and associated with changing teacher professionalism, ethical mediation, governance, structural constraints, and a rapidly expanding but methodologically uneven evidence base. The review rejects purely technical, universal, or tool-centred models of innovation. Instead, it positions AI pedagogy as a context-specific, human-led, competence-rich, and governance-aware form of teaching in which AI supports planning, feedback, adaptation, and reflection without displacing human educational responsibility, especially within teacher education contexts and programmes.

items.title: AI-Assisted Design Judgment: Perceived AI Interaction Conditions, Critical Evaluation of AI Advice, and Expert-Rated Design Judgment Quality
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to analyze and compare design alternatives, yet how design students evaluate AI advice and how such evaluation relates to final design judgments remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the associations among perceived AI interaction conditions, critical evaluation of AI advice, and expert-rated Design Judgment Quality. A cross-sectional study combined a standardized poster comparison task with a post-task questionnaire involving 118 visual communication design students. Participants interacted with Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro and submitted design choices, rationales, and revision recommendations. Perceived Feedback Diagnosticity, Interaction Controllability, and three critical evaluation activities were measured through post-task self-reports, while Design Judgment Quality was independently assessed by three experts. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used for hypothesis testing. Feedback Diagnosticity was positively associated with Evidence Verification, Argument Scrutiny, Contextual Fit Evaluation, and Design Judgment Quality. Interaction Controllability was positively associated with Argument Scrutiny and Contextual Fit Evaluation, but not directly with Design Judgment Quality. Among the three evaluation activities, only Argument Scrutiny showed a significant positive association with expert-rated Design Judgment Quality. These findings suggest that AI-assisted design judgment requires attention to both the perceived value of AI feedback and how users examine AI recommendations and their underlying rationales.

items.title: An Emerging NMR School of Thought: Shared Foundations, Conceptual Architecture, and Autonomous Contributions
items.abstract: This conceptual working paper examines whether the New Human Rights (Neue Menschenrechte, NMR) approach developed by Jean-Pol Martin displays the characteristics of an emerging school of thought.It proposes five analytical criteria: a shared theoretical core, an interconnected vocabulary, a recognizable mode of inquiry, sustained collective activity, and autonomous contributions beyond the founder. Drawing on selected primary texts, publisher descriptions and public practitioner accounts, the paper identifies indications of these features in publications, training activities and distinct applications of the framework.The conceptual architecture connects an organism-based understanding of human beings, six basic need domains, a universal normative commitment to enabling their satisfaction, and a process model linking exploration, information processing, conceptualization and agency. Learning by Teaching (LdL) and human–AI cooperation are situated within this architecture.The article’s specific contribution is to shift attention from an individual theoretical project to the development of a shared intellectual and practical tradition. Within the ongoing sequence of papers on LdL, NMR and human–AI cooperation, it connects the reconstruction of Martin’s work with a prospective collective research programme.The paper distinguishes autonomous development within the project from independent reception outside its originating network. It concludes that “an emerging NMR school of thought” is a defensible interpretation of the documented activities and identifies questions for further conceptual and empirical investigation.Prepared by Jean-Pol Martin in collaboration with ChatGPT. The article includes references and an authorship transparency statement.

items.title: Anatomical Review: Optimizing and Harnessing Workflows — A Section-by-Section Reading of Noguer i Alonso (2026), Task-Specific Combinations of Humans, Software, and AI Agents
items.abstract: This anatomical review systematically dissects Noguer i Alonso's (2026) framework for hybrid workflows integrating human decision makers (H), specified computational procedures (D), and adaptive artificial delegates (A). The paper advances a principled account of agentification, deagentification, automation, and harnessing, grounded in a partial order on delegation profiles rather than scalar autonomy scores, and supported by formal results on permission restriction, invariant preservation, retry exposure, advisory isolation, and the proceduralization gap. While the contribution offers valuable conceptual clarity for task-specific authority allocation in agentic systems, the review identifies limitations in empirical scope (synthetic examples only), the open problem of semantic promotion, and the transferability of formal guarantees to production environments. Implications for AI governance, hybrid intelligence, and institutional design in Global South contexts are discussed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Supply Chain Management: Applications, Evidence, Implementation Constraints, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly investigated as decision-support technologies for supply chain management (SCM), yet their value depends on the nature of the decision, data availability, organisational capability and the methods used to evaluate outcomes. This critical narrative review examines applications across demand forecasting, inventory planning, sourcing, manufacturing, logistics, risk management and sustainability. It brings together relevant peer-reviewed reviews, conceptual contributions and empirical studies, and distinguishes evidence from operational deployments from results reported in literature syntheses or simulations. The literature supports the practical relevance of data-driven prediction, pattern detection and decision augmentation, but it does not establish uniform improvements in cost, forecast accuracy, resilience or environmental performance across settings. Reviewed research also identifies integration costs, fragmented data, process misalignment, model drift, limited transparency and governance concerns as barriers to realising benefits. Recent work on generative AI broadens possible applications to document-intensive processes, synthetic scenarios and interactive decision support, while indicating that field-based validation remains limited. A process-oriented framework is proposed in which analytics inform planning, procurement, manufacturing, distribution and inventory decisions under continuous human oversight. The review argues that useful evaluations should compare AI-supported decisions against relevant operational baselines, account for service levels and cost trade-offs, and document transferability across sectors and resource settings. Future research should prioritise longitudinal field studies, cross-organisational coordination, responsible deployment and context-sensitive applications in emerging economies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Capabilities and Organizational Sustainability of Retail Outlets in Port Harcourt: A Drive for Renewable Hope in Smart Economies
items.abstract: The study examined artificial intelligence capabilities and organizational sustainability of retail outlets in Port Harcourt. The objectives of the study were to examine the relationship between dimensions of artificial intelligence capabilities such as CCTV analytics, chatbots and automated processing; and measures of organizational sustainability in terms of Environmental sustainability and Economic sustainability of retail outlets in Port Harcourt. Thus, the study was anchored on Diffusion of Innovation theoretical foundation. The study adopted the cross-sectional survey research design. The accessible population of the study was Sixteen (16) retail outlets currently operating in Port Harcourt. The entire population was used as the study sample. Thus, the study was census research which involves using the entire population rather than drawing a sample from it. Structured questionnaire served as the instrument for data collection. A total of sixty-four (64) copies of the validated questionnaire were distributed to the targeted audience. The researcher was able to retrieve fifty-six (56) copies of the entire validated questionnaire distributed. Arithmetic mean and standard deviation were used for the research question analyses, while the test of hypotheses was done using Spearman rank order correlation with the aid of SPSS Version 24.0. It was found that there is a significant positive relationship between artificial intelligence capabilities and organizational sustainability of retail outlets in Port Harcourt. It was concluded that leveraging artificial intelligence powered tools such as CCTV analytics, chatbots and automated processing, retailers can enhance operational efficiency, improve customer experiences and gain valuable insights into market trends. Consequently, it was recommended that operators of retail outlets should utilize automated system to track inventory level, reduce waste and optimize stock replenishment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Eurasian Higher Education: An Empirical Study of Student Practices
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has penetrated higher education not through official strategies but via students’ and faculty members’ personal devices, catching most universities off guard. This article presents empirical data from a large-scale survey conducted between March and April 2026 across six post-Soviet countries (Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Tajikistan). The study provides a systematic cross-national analysis of student AI use patterns in the Eurasian higher education space, complementing recent single-country studies in the region. The sample included 478 students. The study measured frequency of AI use, perceived risks, compatibility with educational values, and the presence of institutional regulatory mechanisms. The results show that 78 % of students regularly use generative AI, yet only 32 % of universities have an official policy in this area. A deep disciplinary divide emerges: students fall into two roughly equal profiles – “pragmatic techs” (daily users with low ethical anxiety) and “reflective humanists” (cautious users with a strong demand for ethical frameworks). The main barrier to AI adoption is not technological infrastructure but the absence of regulatory and social technologies. The article offers discipline-differentiated recommendations for universities in non-Western contexts.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE RISK GOVERNANCE AND REGULATORY COMPLIANCE: A GLOBAL LEGAL PERSPECTIVE
items.abstract: The swift spread of Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the realms of medicine, banking, hiring practices, law enforcement, and governmental administration has led to the emergence of a new type of legal risk that the conventional mechanisms of regulation are poorly designed to tackle. Such dynamic, data-driven, opaque, and increasingly self-reliant technologies pose difficulties when it comes to apportioning legal responsibilities and ensuring individuals' rights. In this paper, I provide a doctrinal and comparative review of the responses to AI-related risks developed by major jurisdictions – the EU, the USA, the UK, and China – as well as by international organizations, namely the OECD, UNESCO, and UN. In my work, I follow the development of the global AI governance system from ethical guidelines to risk-based regulatory compliance, and explore the most important legal issues, including algorithmic bias, data protection, transparency, cybersecurity, liability, and misinformation generated by generative AI models. Based on this comparative analysis, the paper presents an innovative six-stage AI Risk Governance and Compliance Framework rooted in the concepts of risk proportionality, lifecycle governance, human accountability, transparency, continuous compliance, and international cooperation. It is contended that a single national framework is not enough and that an effective global AI governance system requires a hybrid framework which combines the EU’s systematic risk categorization system, US’ flexible sectoral approach, UK’s adaptable regulator-led framework, and international soft law instruments’ human rights focus.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Use in Honours Research: Implications for Supervision Relationships, Knowledge Development, and Research Quality
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has reshaped how students engage with academic research, particularly at Honours level, where students transition from structured undergraduate learning to independent postgraduate research. Guided by Self‑Regulated Learning (SRL) theory, this study examines how reliance on AI by Honours research students influences the supervisor-supervisee relationship, the quality of research produced, and the extent of knowledge gained through the research process. SRL theory emphasises learners’ ability to plan, monitor, and reflect on their own learning, which is central to successful postgraduate research development. This study adopts a conceptual and literature‑based review methodology, drawing on peer‑reviewed studies on AI use in higher education, literature on postgraduate supervision, and academic integrity and research skills development frameworks, with specific attention to Honours‑level contexts. The documents were analysed using thematic content analysis, focusing on self‑regulatory behaviours, supervisory interaction, research skill development, and learning depth. The findings suggest that limited and transparent use of AI can support honours students by reducing surface‑level cognitive load and assisting with language clarity. However, excessive reliance on AI may undermine key self‑regulation processes, weaken critical thinking, and reduce meaningful engagement with supervisors. Supervisors may struggle to accurately assess students’ understanding, potentially straining trust and feedback processes. The review further indicates that over‑reliance on AI risks producing research that is technically adequate but conceptually shallow, with reduced long‑term knowledge acquisition. The study concludes that clear supervision practices and explicit guidance on responsible AI use are necessary to ensure that AI supports, rather than replaces, the self‑regulated learning essential for high‑quality Honours‑level research.

items.title: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI
items.abstract: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.

items.title: Beyond Automation: Human–Technology Synergy and the Future of Work
items.abstract: Rapid technological advancement is transforming contemporary organizations and reshaping the future of work. Artificial intelligence (AI), automation, digital communication technologies, and data-driven systems increasingly influence organizational structures, managerial practices, employee experiences, and workplace interactions. While these developments offer important opportunities to improve efficiency, flexibility, and innovation, they also raise significant concerns about employee well-being, ethical responsibility, privacy, surveillance, and workforce adaptation. This chapter examines the evolving relationship between humans and technology from a human-centered perspective. First, it briefly discusses the historical evolution of workplace technologies, from the Industrial Revolution to the current era of AI-driven digital transformation. Second, the chapter explores human–technology synergy and emphasizes the importance of collaboration and complementarity between human and technological capabilities in organizational settings. Third, it examines the growing role of human-centered technology in supporting employee well-being, inclusivity, participation, and ethical organizational practices. The chapter also discusses the organizational implications of AI integration, including changes in job roles, decision-making processes, workplace flexibility, and employee adaptation. Finally, key challenges associated with technology integration, such as algorithmic bias, workplace surveillance, digital fatigue, and technological dependency, are addressed alongside potential future directions of human–technology collaboration. Overall, the chapter argues that successful digital transformation requires organizations to balance technological advancement with human values, needs, and capabilities. The long-term sustainability of workplace technologies depends not only on operational efficiency but also on organizations’ ability to foster ethical, adaptive, and mutually beneficial relationships between humans and technology.

items.title: Commercial Dungeness Crab Fishermen’s Perceptions of Exoskeleton Use to Reduce Musculoskeletal Injuries
items.abstract: Commercial crab fishing involves physically demanding tasks that increase the risk of work-related musculoskeletal disorders. This study evaluated fishermen’s perceptions of occupational exoskeletons as a potential intervention to reduce physical demands in commercial fishing. Twenty commercial crab fishermen completed an in-person survey after trying soft and/or rigid exoskeletons. The survey assessed fishermen’s demographics and work characteristics, awareness, adoption and acceptance factors, potential applications, and perceived barriers to exoskeleton use. Descriptive statistics and content analysis were used to summarize responses. Fishermen identified practicality as the key adoption factor and shared concerns about cost, time required to don and doff the device, bulkiness, and incompatibility with rain gear. Crab pot handling and crab sorting were identified as potential use cases. Overall, fishermen viewed exoskeletons as potentially useful for reducing physical demands during commercial crabbing; however, successful adoption will require lightweight, comfortable, and affordable designs compatible with fishing gear and challenging work conditions.
